description.narrative:
Geneva Call har ansökt till Sida om kärnstöd om 30 miljoner kr för perioden 2020-2022 för att genomföra organisationens övergripande strategiska plan.
Den strategiska planen anger Geneva Calls humanitära engagemang med icke-statliga väpnade aktörer i syfte att stärka skydd av civila i konfliktkontexter. De tematiska områdena är förbud mot antipersonella minor och samarbete kring minhantering, skydd av barn från effekter av väpnad konflikt, förbud mot sexuellt våld i väpnade konflikter and mot elimineringen av könsdiskriminering, skydd av kulturellt arv i väpnade konflikter, skydd av hälsovård, samt förbud mot tvångsförflyttningar. Organisationen är för närvarande aktiv i 13 kontexer och har kontor i 12 av dem (Jemen, Irak, Colombia, Syrien, Demokratiska Republiken Kongo, Mali, Libanon, Filippinerna, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Ukraina och Sydsudan).
Geneva Calls totala budget är 410 miljoner kr. Sidas kärnstöd täcker ungefär 10 procent av det totala behovet per år och cirka 50 procent av kärnstödet. Övriga huvudsakliga givare är Schweiz, ECHO och Norge.

Geneva Call has applied to Sida for core funding of 30 million SEK for 2020-2022 to implement its Strategic Plan.
The Strategic Plan outlines Geneva Call's humanitarian engagement with Armed non-State actors (ANSAs) towards better protection of civilians in situations of conflict. Thematic areas are the ban on antipersonnel mines and cooperation in mine action; the protection of children from the effects of armed conflict; the prohibition of sexual violence in situations of armed conflict and the work towards the elimination of gender discrimination; the protection of cultural heritage in armed conflict; the protection of health care; and the prohibition of forced displacement. The organisation is currently active in 13 contexts and has offices in 12 of them (Yemen, Iraq, Colombia, Syria, the DRC, Mali, Lebanon, the Philippines, Afghanistan, Myanmar, South Sudan and Ukraine).
Geneva Call's total budget is 410 million SEK. The Sida core support covers roughly 10 percent of the total need per year and about 50 percent of the current core support. Other key donors are Switzerland, ECHO and Norway.

To contribute towards the improved protection of civilians in armed conflicts, through the increased respect for humanitarian norms by Armed Non-State Actors (ANSAs), for the period 2020-2023, Geneva Call will: - Deepen expertise on the engagement of ANSAs and consolidate its action on the ground; - Strengthen Geneva Calls capacity to implement its operations effectively and sustainably.

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
Results achieved in 2023:
Overall, results are reported at various levels of impact for conflict affected populations, policy changes, coordination and humanitarian engagement for access etc. There are several useful examples of how GC's work has influenced and at times contributed to drastic (and encouraging) changes in AGDAs' conflict behaviour. This includes the evacuation of civilian infrastructure such as schools and allowing access to farming lands in Burkina Faso (allowing thousands of children access to their education since a dozen of schools were evacuated); improvement in allowing humanitarian access in countries such as Sudan and the negotiating of release of aid organisations' vehicles at check points in eg. Yemen. Relevant examples also come from Afghanistan where training of IEA police officers has yielded reported increased respect of individuals' human rights at check points and extensive engagement and policy reinforcement in Syria and Iraq led to the restitution of civilian properties when armed groups pulled back from occupied buildings, likely an important corner stone for future transitional justice efforts in these countries. In South Sudan, Sida notes that important steps have been taken on respecting individuals' rights to protection through foremost some AGDAs decreasing harassment of women and demilitarizing civilian residential areas. This has benefited several thousands of people according to the annual report.
Examples of results at country level:
- In Colombia numerous communities have reported changes in AGDAs behaviour when it comes to refraining from using schools as targets for mobilization or headquarters. This has led to increased child protection, lessening the risk of child recruitment and making schools and communities safer overall.
- In Burkina Faso impact is seen in different areas and at different levels, e.g. through the humanitarian engagement with self-defense groups three Unilateral Declarations signed in 2022 on child protection has led to concrete measures taken by these same groups. For example adoption of age verification measures and relocation of more than 15 of their military bases led to that 21 schools were able to reopen between 2022 and 2023 in three regions. The work in BF has also addressed a protocol that the groups signed on humane treatment of detained women and girls during hostilities and in order to promote food security, self defense groups of the Dozo's set up groups patrolling to protect farmers during the growing season that enabled them safe cultivating and harvesting.
- For the DR Congo there are several examples of how the engagement with AGDAs led to three unilateral declarations on SGBV and food insecurity for example. Concrete results include the liberation of four occupied schools, the release of humanitarian, medical and educational personnel held in captivity and relocation of military positions away from civilian infrastructure. It seems that careful community engagement has contributed to the development of self-protection mechanisms e.g. creation of roadmaps that allowed for AGDAs to collect taxes with better methods and using these to invest in pubic infrastructure.
- For Ukraine most of the significant results during 2023 are related to trainings and increased awareness of IHL where GC has used various methods to reach far beyond 2,000 combatants on both sides. The trainings were based on analysis of the key IHL application gaps, a survey conducted post-training revealed that over 75 % indicated they felt that the activity had significantly influenced their combat decision-making. Telling for the complex, volatile context the main challenges in the work are related to that combatants are often hard to reach due to their active role in in ongoing battles, the security risks re to work in active combat areas for GC, as well as the polarization of the conflict making it challenging for principled humanitarian action to take place, on both side of the front line.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
